# Nurse Staffing and Patient Outcomes: Evidence for a Staffing Policy Decision

## Adequate nurse staffing is the most evidence-backed lever a hospital COO holds for reducing deaths and costs

The decision before you is whether to commit to enforceable minimum nurse-to-patient ratios or to continue flexible, market-driven staffing. The evidence from multiple independent sources points to one answer: committing to adequate ratios reduces patient deaths, lowers operating costs, and stabilizes your workforce. A hospital that understaffs its nursing teams pays for that choice in preventable mortality, longer stays, and clinician turnover. [S35] [S36] [S38]

> "In New York, if hospitals followed the 4:1 patient-to-nurse ratio, they would have saved 4,370 lives and $720 million in just two years." [S35]

The financial case is not a trade-off against quality. In New York, a hospital system operating at a mandated ratio would have avoided a large number of deaths and saved a substantial sum over a multi-year period. In Illinois, the same ratio would have prevented a comparable scale of deaths and saved a similar amount within a year. A COO who treats staffing as a pure cost line is misreading the economics. [S35] [S37]

> "In Illinois, staffing ratios could have prevented 1,595 deaths, and hospitals could have saved $117 million in just one year." [S35]

> "The 2021 study of hospital medical surgical units in Illinois found that a staffing ratio of four patients to one nurse would have saved a total of $117 million per year across the hospitals in the study due to reduced lengths of stay." [S37]

The American Nurses Association states that the evidence base supports appropriate staffing as a driver of better outcomes and higher satisfaction for both patients and nurses. This is not a partisan or union position; it is a clinical and financial conclusion that a COO can act on directly. [S38]

> "Evidence shows appropriate nurse staffing contributes to improved patient outcomes and greater satisfaction for both patients and nurses." [S38]

## Each additional patient on a nurse's assignment raises the risk of death

A study cited by the American Federation of Teachers found that each additional patient assigned to a nurse's workload is associated with a measurable increase in the risk of hospital mortality and failure to rescue. For a hospital COO, this means that every patient added beyond a safe threshold is not a neutral scheduling decision; it is a direct increase in the probability that a patient will die. [S36]

> "research conducted by my colleagues and me established that each one patient added to a nurse’s workload is associated with a 7 percent increase in the risk of hospital mortality and failure to rescue patients." [S36]

A 2021 study of medical-surgical units in Illinois found a steeper effect: for each additional patient on a nurse's average workload, the likelihood of the patient dying within a defined post-admission window increased substantially, and the likelihood of a longer hospital stay also rose. This is a different metric from the hospital-mortality measure in the earlier study, and the two findings are not in conflict; they measure different windows and different endpoints. [S37]

> "A 2021 study found that in hospital medical surgical units in Illinois, for each patient added to a nurse’s average workload, the likelihood of the patient dying within 30 days of admission increased by 16 percent, and the likelihood that the patient stayed in the hospital for a day longer increased by five percent." [S37]

The two studies use different populations and different outcome windows, so the exact magnitude differs. What is consistent across both is the direction and the mechanism: more patients per nurse, worse survival. This is an inference drawn from the two studies, not a direct finding of either, but it is the pattern a COO should plan around. [S36] [S37]

## Understaffing does not save money; it transfers cost to complications and turnover

Multiple rigorous studies have documented that replacing registered nurses with lower-qualified personnel produces worse patient outcomes and does not reduce costs, because the savings in wages are offset by increased complications and higher turnover. A COO who substitutes lower-cost staff to close a budget gap is, in effect, deferring a larger expense. [S36]

> "Many rigorous studies have documented that replacing RNs with lower-qualified personnel results in poor patient outcomes and poor RN retention, and it does not save money." [S36]

The Illinois study estimated that a mandated staffing ratio would have saved a substantial annual sum across the hospitals in the study, driven by reduced lengths of stay. The New York analysis reached a similar conclusion over a longer period. The mechanism is straightforward: fewer complications, shorter stays, lower per-patient cost. [S35] [S37]

> "In New York, if hospitals followed the 4:1 patient-to-nurse ratio, they would have saved 4,370 lives and $720 million in just two years." [S35]

A 2024 study by the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that hospitals had been increasing their use of supplemental nurses, with the rise ranging widely across the institutions studied. This suggests that the industry is already responding to a staffing gap, but the variation implies that the response is uneven and not yet systematic. A COO who waits for a regulator to mandate ratios is ceding control of that cost to a future policy cycle. [S37]

> "A 2024 study by the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that among the hospitals studied, the increase in the number of supplemental nurses from 2019 to 2022 ranged from two to 28 percent." [S37]

## Understaffing drives burnout, turnover, and poor safety ratings

A 2023 study involving nurses and physicians at Magnet hospitals across the United States found that hospitals with too few nurses and unfavorable work environments had higher rates of clinician burnout, turnover, and unfavorable patient safety ratings. For a COO, this means that a staffing shortfall is not only a patient-safety problem; it is a workforce-retention problem that compounds year over year. [S37]

> "A 2023 study involving both nurses and physicians at 60 Magnet hospitals across the U.S. found that nurse staffing was the primary issue that subjects identified as wanting management to improve. Additionally, the study revealed that 'hospitals characterized as having too few nurses and unfavorable work environments had higher rates of clinician burnout, turnover, and unfavorable patient safety ratings.'" [S37]

Numerous studies reveal an association between higher levels of experienced registered nurse staffing and lower rates of adverse patient outcomes. The implication for a hospital COO is that the quality of the staffing mix, not just the headcount, determines whether patients are safe. A COO who hires to fill a shift but ignores experience and competency is not solving the underlying risk. [S38]

> "Numerous studies reveal an association between higher levels of experienced RN staffing and lower rates of adverse patient outcomes." [S38]

Healthgrades medical advisor Alana Biggers states that hospitals must invest in workforce development and support, including ensuring appropriate staffing levels, to provide high-quality care. When teams are adequately supported, they communicate better with patients and coordinate care more effectively. This is a quality-and-experience argument that a COO can bring to a board focused on patient-satisfaction scores. [S41]

> "I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development" [S41]

## The evidence supports enforceable ratios as a policy lever, not just a guideline

The American Nurses Association supports enforceable minimum nurse-to-patient ratios as an essential approach to achieving appropriate staffing. For a hospital COO, this means that a voluntary internal target is weaker than a binding standard, because voluntary targets are the first line item cut when revenue dips. A COO who wants the staffing level to survive a budget cycle should advocate for a ratio that is enforceable, not merely recommended. [S38]

> "The American Nurses Association (ANA) supports enforceable ratios as an essential approach to achieving appropriate nurse staffing ." [S38]

The evidence base is broad enough to support a policy decision now. Multiple independent studies, spanning different states, different unit types, and different outcome measures, all point in the same direction. A COO does not need to wait for a single definitive trial; the pattern is consistent across the sources available. [S36] [S37] [S38]

## Commit to a minimum ratio now, and revisit only if a credible hospital-specific cost model shows otherwise

A hospital COO should set an enforceable minimum nurse-to-patient ratio for medical-surgical units, align it with the ratio standard that the Illinois and New York analyses show would have prevented deaths and saved money, and build the ratio into the annual budget as a fixed cost rather than a variable. The condition under which the alternative, a flexible staffing model, would be defensible is if a hospital-specific cost model demonstrates that the local complication rate, length-of-stay distribution, and turnover costs do not follow the pattern seen in the studies cited here. [S35] [S37]

> "The same study estimated that if the hospitals were staffed at four patients to one nurse during the study period, 'more than 1595 deaths would have been avoided.'" [S37]

Until that hospital-specific model exists, the default should be the ratio. The cost of inaction is not a line item on a spreadsheet; it is a preventable death on a unit that the COO manages. The evidence does not require a COO to choose between fiscal discipline and patient safety, because the two are the same decision. [S36] [S38]
